thesis: Lululemon has already cut guidance twice this year and now guides FY2026 EPS to $10.95-$11.15, putting the stock at roughly 11x its own lowered numbers at 121.07, against a 52-week range of 104.44 to 225.98. The confirmation is the insider record: chairman Charles V Bergh, the former Levi Strauss CEO, bought 6,090 shares at $164.20 in March and then bought 4,275 MORE at $117.05 in June - doubling down 29% lower - with Andre Maestrini buying 3,275 at $151.02 between them. Three open-market purchases, two buyers, $1.99M bought against $0.10M sold. The de-rating is a merchandising and China problem, not a broken franchise, and the reset has already been published rather than being ahead of the market.
key_risk: The invalidation is fundamental, not a price level: gross margin below 55% for two consecutive quarters, or a third guidance cut taking FY2027 EPS below $10, would mean the brand is losing pricing power rather than working through a bad product cycle - 11x on a number that keeps falling is not cheap. Note also that Bergh is underwater on both purchases, so the insider signal is conviction rather than timing, and this is the second athletic-apparel de-rating in the report alongside NKE.
counter_argument: A lower valuation does not fix the problem. Lululemon is down 42% YTD and 49% from its all-time high precisely because each reset has been followed by another, Q2 revenue is guided to decline 2-3% year over year, and Q2 EPS of $1.76-$1.81 against $3.10 a year ago is a 42% collapse in earnings power. Value investors - including the chairman - have been early on this name all year.

thesis: IBM lost about $69B of market value in a single session on a 2.7% EPS miss and a 3.7% revenue miss - the worst day in its history, worse than October 1987 - and CEO Arvind Krishna gave a specific, checkable reason: in the final weeks of June, clients redirected budget from IBM software and infrastructure toward servers, storage and memory chips to lock in supply-constrained hardware ahead of price increases, and large deals slipped past their expected close dates. Budget that moves forward a quarter to beat a price increase is deferred revenue, not lost revenue. The stock has since held a tight 228.85-238.42 range for three weeks, so the forced selling is finished and what remains is a question about whether those deals close.
key_risk: The invalidation is precise and dated to the reports rather than the price: if Q3 and Q4 software revenue does not recover the deals that slipped out of Q2, then the shift was share loss dressed up as timing and IBM breaks its 199.19 post-crash low. The market clearly leans that way - a 25% reaction to a 3.7% miss is a verdict on forward execution, not on one quarter - and the CEO has publicly conceded the company fell behind. Note also there is no insider support here: the only two open-market buys totalled $113K and predate the crash.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is simply the size of the reaction. Markets do not erase $69B over a rounding error unless they have decided the growth story is broken, and a CEO who did not see a spending shift coming three weeks before quarter-end is telling you something about the visibility of the pipeline. If enterprise budget is structurally migrating from IBM software to hardware in an AI buildout, no amount of deal-timing arithmetic saves the multiple.
